background.definition: Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis is an infection involving the skin and soft tissue surrounding the eye, but anterior to the orbital septum. Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis is an infection involving the skin and soft tissue posterior to the orbital septum. This topic does not cover other types of cellulitis; see Cellulitis (non-orbital) for cellulitis in general.

list.listitem: Trauma.
Acute sinusitis.
Transient bacteremia.
Insect bite.
Conjunctivitis.
Blepharitis.
Dental infection.
Most common bacterial organisms are Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and anaerobes.
Since the introduction of the Haemophilus influenzae type B vaccination, periorbital and orbital cellulitis due to Haemophilus influenzae has declined.
Periorbital cellulitis: Infection of the skin and soft tissue surrounding the eye, often introduced by a minor trauma (scratch, bug bite) or extension of infection from acute sinusitis.
Blockage of venous and lymphatic drainage leads to eyelid edema.
Orbital cellulitis: Infection extends past the orbital septum, leading to proptosis, limitation of eye movement, and some visual disturbance.
Pus forms between the orbit and sinus periosteum, leading to more proptosis and vision loss.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis may result.
Since the introduction of the Haemophilus influenzae type B vaccination, periorbital and orbital cellulitis due to Haemophilus influenzae type B has declined. B
Periorbital cellulitis should be suspected if fever accompanies unilateral eyelid erythema and swelling. C
Orbital cellulitis should be suspected if fever, proptosis, pain or limitation of extraocular movements, and visual loss accompany unilateral eyelid erythema and swelling. C
If orbital cellulitis is suspected, an orbital CT with contrast should be performed promptly. C
If contralateral eyelid erythema, edema, ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, or vision loss occurs, MRI should be performed to evaluate for cavernous sinus thrombosis. C

list.listitem: Periorbital cellulitis usually presents with unilateral swelling, erythema, and tenderness of the upper and lower eyelids. The patient may or may not have fever (see ).
Orbital cellulitis can often present like periorbital cellulitis, but the patient may also have pain or limitation of extraocular movement, proptosis, and visual loss.
It may be difficult to distinguish periorbital from orbital cellulitis, especially in young children. When in doubt, or if periorbital cellulitis is severe, hospitalize and administer IV antibiotics.
White blood cell count is not a very sensitive test to distinguish between periorbital and orbital cellulitis.
Orbital computed tomography (CT) with contrast will help distinguish between periorbital and orbital cellulitis.
Suspect a dental origin of the orbital cellulitis if the CT scan shows abnormal periapical lucency, widening of the periodontal ligament space, and a subperiosteal abscess.
Suspect a sinus origin of the orbital cellulitis if the CT scan shows sinus disease.
Obtain an MRI if cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected.
See the algorithm in .
Children with possible orbital cellulitis should be hospitalized for IV antibiotics and closely monitored by an otolaryngologist or ophthalmologist. C
Periorbital cellulitis should be treated with oral antibiotics and close follow-up. C

If patients do not improve or deteriorate within 24 hours of oral antibiotics, or if they present with severe disease (eg, >50% eyelid closure), they should be hospitalized for IV antibiotics, close monitoring, and orbital CT. C

Empiric IV antibiotics should be initiated if orbital cellulitis is suspected. Staphylococcus and Streptococcus are common organisms, so second- or third-generation cephalosporins, or ampicillin/sulbactam should be started. Nafcillin may be considered (see ).
IV antibiotics can be switched to oral antibiotics to complete a 10- to 14-day course once the eyelid edema and erythema have significantly improved.
If anaerobes are suspected (from a sinus or odontogenic source), consider clindamycin or metronidazole for better anaerobic coverage.

Community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) as a cause of periorbital/orbital cellulitis is increasing, so consider vancomycin for orbital cellulitis that is poorly responsive to antibiotics.

Oral antibiotics should be initiated if periorbital cellulitis is suspected (). High-dose amoxicillin, high-dose augmentin, or cefuroxime axetil for 10 to 14 days will cover most Streptococcus and Staphylococcus. If MRSA is suspected, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or clindamycin (depending on local susceptibilities) should be started.
If periorbital cellulitis is severe (>50% of eyelid closed), consider hospitalization with IV antibiotics ().

A 10- to 14-day course is usually sufficient, even if associated with sinusitis. Patients treated with oral antibiotics for presumed periorbital cellulitis should be followed closely (daily follow-up until improvement occurs) for response to antibiotics and possible progression to orbital cellulitis.

A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of systemic corticosteroids in addition to systemic antibiotics for the treatment of periorbital and orbital cellulitis. Only 1 RCT with 21 participants was included in the review, and it suffered from significant methodological flaws.

Grade III or higher orbital cellulitis (where there is periosteal or orbital abscess formation) may require incision and debridement by otolaryngology or ophthalmology if not improving with IV antibiotics (see and ).

The likelihood of surgical intervention increases with the following risk factors: age older than 9 years, proptosis, extraocular motility restriction, and elevated intraocular pressure, from 7% (95% CI: 1%-13%) with zero risk factors, to 95% (95% CI: 89%-100%) with all 4 risk factors.
For patients that appear to present with orbital cellulitis, it is important to consult otolaryngology or ophthalmology.
Patients diagnosed with orbital cellulitis should be hospitalized for IV antibiotics and closely monitored with the assistance of otolaryngology or ophthalmology.
Patients with rapid progression of periorbital cellulitis or are not responding to oral antibiotics within 24 hours should be hospitalized for IV antibiotics and closely monitored.
A study of 89 children found that those with more symptoms and fever were more likely to be admitted.
Orbital cellulitis may lead to permanent vision loss (0%-29%), neurologic deficits (0%-17%), or death (0%-3%). B

feature.caption: Staging of Orbital Cellulitis-Modified Chandler Classification.
feature.feature_body:
Group Category Description
I Periorbital cellulitis Eyelid edema and erythema. Normal extraocular movements. Normal visual acuity. CT shows inflammatory soft-tissue thickening of orbit anterior to orbital septum. Occasionally chemosis.
II Orbital cellulitis Proptosis, chemosis, decreased extraocular movement, rarely visual loss. CT shows diffuse edema of orbital contents. No discrete abscess.
III Subperiosteal abscess Proptosis with downward and lateral globe displacement. Occasionally visual loss. CT shows subperiosteal abscess between periorbita and involved sinus.
IV Orbital abscess Proptosis, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia, decreased visual acuity. CT shows orbital abscess.
V Cavernous sinus thrombosis (complication of orbital cellulitis) Proptosis and ophthalmoplegia with development of similar signs on contralateral side, retinal engorgement, visual loss. CT or MRI shows cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Adapted from Staging of orbital cellulitis. Mafee MF, Valvassori GE, Becker M, Lewin JS. Imaging of the Head and Neck. 2nd. New York: Thieme Medical Publications; 1995.

feature.caption: Antibiotic Choices for Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis.
feature.feature_body:
Antibiotic Comments
Periorbital cellulitis PO high-dose amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (80-90 mg/kg divided bid; max 875/125 mg bid), cefuroxime axetil (30 mg/kg/day divided bid; max 500 mg bid), cefdinir (14 mg/kg/day daily; max 600 mg daily), or cefpodoxime (10 mg/kg/day divided bid; max 400 mg bid) for 10-14 days. If mod/severe, treat with IV antibiotics as below.
If anaerobes are likely, consider PO clindamycin (30 mg/kg/day divided 3 times a day; max 4.8 g/day) or metronidazole (30 mg/kg/day divided qid; max 4 g/day).
If MRSA is suspected, consider PO clindamycin or Bactrim (8-10 mg/kg/day divided bid) (depending on local susceptibilities).
Orbital cellulitis IV ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day divided bid), ampicillin/sulbactam (200 mg/kg/day divided qid). If anaerobes are likely, consider adding IV clindamycin (40 mg/kg/day divided 3 times a day) or metronidazole (30 mg/kg/day divided qid; max 4 g/day).
If MRSA is suspected, consider IV vancomycin (60 mg/kg/day divided qid).
May switch to PO antibiotics to finish the 10- to 14-day course once orbital cellulitis is clinically improved.
Data from American Academy of Pediatrics. Subcommittee on Management of Sinusitis and Committee on Quality Improvement. Clinical practice guideline: management of sinusitis. Pediatrics. 2001;108:798-808; and Howe L, Jones NS. Guidelines for the management of periorbital cellulitis/abscess. Clin Otolaryngol Allied Sci. 2004;29:725-728.
